questions.q: What is `gs` in a server-side script?
options: The GlideSystem global object, available automatically in every server-side script
A variable you must declare yourself before using it
An object only available inside Client Scripts
A deprecated API that no longer works on current ServiceNow instances
questions.explain: GlideSystem (gs) is available automatically wherever server-side script runs — Business Rules, Script Includes, Scheduled Jobs.

questions.q:
What does this line actually do?

gs.info('Priority change: ' + oldPriority + ' -> ' + newPriority, 'EscalationRule');
options: Writes a row into the System Log, with the message and 'EscalationRule' as the source, so it can be filtered and found later
Changes the incident's priority field directly to the new value
Throws an error unless oldPriority and newPriority are equal
Sends an email to the assigned user with the priority change
questions.explain: gs.info() only logs — it writes a row to syslog with an optional source string. It never modifies a record on its own.

questions.q: What is the relationship between `gs.log()` and `gs.info()`?
options: gs.log() is the older method, equivalent to info-level logging, still common in legacy scripts
gs.log() only works in Client Scripts, while gs.info() only works on the server
gs.log() logs at error severity, while gs.info() does nothing at all
They write to two completely different, unrelated tables
questions.explain: gs.log() predates gs.info()/gs.warn()/gs.error() but produces the same info-level result — both ultimately write to syslog.

questions.q: Which table do gs.info(), gs.warn(), and gs.error() actually write their messages into?
options: The syslog table — the System Log covered back in Course 3
The incident table
A temporary table that is cleared at the end of every transaction
No table at all; the messages exist only in server memory
questions.explain: Every logging call from gs ultimately inserts a row into syslog, the same table you already know how to query with GlideRecord.

questions.q: A Business Rule is configured to run asynchronously, so the Script Debugger can't attach to it. What's the practical workflow to figure out what it actually did?
options: Add gs.info() calls at key points in the script, trigger it, then filter the System Log by the source string and the time window it ran in
There is no way to debug an asynchronous Business Rule at all
Switch the rule to run synchronously permanently, even in production
Rewrite the rule entirely in a different scripting language
questions.explain: Since you can't pause async execution live, sprinkling gs.info() calls and reading them back from the System Log afterward is the real, standard workaround.
